title: SQL is not relational algebra
objective: Predict, before each run, the row count and stored values of cells that involve NULL and duplicate rows, and pick a row that a predicate and its negation both skip.

blocks.md: Your transfer lived in a model where a comparison is true or false. Stage 6 compiles it into SQL, and SQL has a third answer. Commit to one prediction before the first cell.

choice.prompt: A table `t(id int, team int, bal bigint CHECK (bal >= 0))` holds rows. Which statement is true?

options.text: Inserting a row whose `bal` is NULL is rejected.
options.why: The manual says a check constraint "is satisfied if the check expression evaluates to true or the null value".

options.text: `SELECT count(bal)` counts the rows whose `bal` is NULL.
`WHERE NOT (bal >= 10)` selects exactly the rows that `WHERE bal >= 10` skips.
options.why: A NULL row makes both predicates unknown, so it lands in neither.

options.text: `SELECT team FROM t` can return the same value twice.
options.why: Tables and results are bags. A plain SELECT keeps duplicates.

blocks.md: **How the cells work.** Every cell in this stage runs PostgreSQL in your browser tab through PGlite 0.5.11, whose `version()` names the same PostgreSQL release as the Bench server, 18.6 {{run:RUN-pglite-0511}}. A cell starts from an empty database, runs its statements in order, and prints each statement's rows, row count or error code. Nothing carries over to the next cell. The tab has one connection, so it cannot show two transactions at once; S6.L6 replays recorded histories for that. While the engine loads, a cell shows a recorded run with its ID.
Two rows, one with a NULL balance and one with 50. The UPDATE debits 10 from every row whose balance is at least 10.
blocks.direction: The cell asserts nothing. It records what the database does: read the row count the UPDATE reports and the balances the SELECT shows.

call.prompt: `UPDATE t SET bal = bal - 10 WHERE bal >= 10` runs over row 1 (balance NULL) and row 2 (balance 50). What happens?

options.text: 1 row: row 2 becomes 40 and the NULL row is untouched.
options.why: `NULL >= 10` is unknown, WHERE keeps only true rows, and nothing reports the skip.

options.text: 0 rows: the NULL row stops the statement.
options.why: WHERE filters row by row, so one unknown row does not fail the statement.

options.text: 2 rows: row 1 stays NULL and row 2 becomes 40.
options.why: An unknown predicate is not true, so row 1 is never selected and never counted.

options.text: An error: NULL cannot be compared with 10.
options.why: Comparing with NULL gives unknown, never an error.

blocks.after: The INSERT put a NULL balance past `CHECK (bal >= 0)`, and the UPDATE skipped that row without a word. SQL has three truth values. A constraint lets unknown through; a filter throws it away. Neither tells you. {{run:RUN-pg-anomalies}}

blocks.md: A `CHECK` accepts a row when its expression is true or unknown. A `WHERE` keeps a row only when its expression is true. So one NULL balance gets past the constraint, and then every guard you write skips it. Two more departures from the algebra you learned: a table is a bag, so a result can repeat a row, and `count(bal)` skips NULLs where `count(*)` does not.
Run it and check each result against the rule above.
blocks.direction: Free run. Predicate, negation and IS NULL together account for every row; the NULL amount selects nothing; `team` repeats.

choice.prompt: A table `t(bal bigint, frozen boolean)` may hold any of the rows below, written `(bal, frozen)`. Which row is selected by neither `WHERE bal >= 10 OR frozen` nor `WHERE NOT (bal >= 10 OR frozen)`?

options.why: `unknown OR true` is true, so the first query selects it.
`false OR unknown` is unknown, and so is its negation. Neither query keeps the row.
`true OR unknown` is true, so the first query selects it.
`false OR false` is false, so the second query selects it.

options.text: `bal = NULL` is true for a NULL `bal`, just as `1 = 1` is true.
options.why: `=` with a NULL operand is unknown. Ask `bal IS NULL`.

options.text: `UNION` keeps duplicate rows, as `UNION ALL` does.
`count(*)` skips rows whose balance is NULL, as `count(bal)` does.
`2 NOT IN (1, NULL)` is unknown and keeps nothing in a `WHERE`.
options.why: `NOT IN` becomes `NOT (2 = 1 OR 2 = NULL)`, which is `NOT unknown`.

RUN-pg-anomalies.title: PostgreSQL 18.6: the isolation table of RESULTS.md (conditional UPDATE, read-modify-write, write skew, NULL, 22003)
verdict_lines: ## PostgreSQL 18.6 (docker `postgres:18`), script: `spikes/pg_anomalies.py` (psycopg 3)

| Two concurrent `UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 80 WHERE id=1 AND bal >= 80` from bal=100 | READ COMMITTED | both statements "ok"; second re-evaluates WHERE on the new row version (EvalPlanQual), updates 0 rows; final bal **20** — **no lost update** |
| App-level read-modify-write: both `SELECT bal` (100), both `UPDATE … SET bal = <read>-80` | READ COMMITTED | final bal **20**, but **160 spent from 100** — lost update / double spend |
| Same read-modify-write | REPEATABLE READ | second writer: **SerializationFailure, SQLSTATE 40001**; final 20 |
| Write skew: invariant sum(team) ≥ 0, each txn checks sum (200) then withdraws 150 from a *different* account | REPEATABLE READ | **both commit; team total −100** |
| Same write skew | SERIALIZABLE | t1 commits, t2 **40001**; total 50 |
| `CHECK (bal >= 0)` with `INSERT … (NULL)` | — | **accepted** (CHECK passes on NULL/unknown) |
| `UPDATE … SET bal = bal - 10 WHERE bal >= 10` over rows {NULL, 50} | — | only the non-NULL row updated; the NULL row is **silently skipped** |
| `9223372036854775807::bigint + 1` | — | **error 22003 "bigint out of range"** — Postgres raises, it does not wrap |

notes: First-load sizes are what the engine requested on a cold load of a page whose module worker imports PGlite and makes one query; the page and worker files are excluded. Wire sizes are gzip bodies made on the host with stock zlib at level 5, the level at which GitHub Pages' gzip output matched byte for byte on four probed public files; GitHub Pages sent gzip and no Brotli to a client that offered both.

No `.data` file was probed and no file as large as pglite.wasm was probed (the probed files are under 1 MB), so the host's behavior for a 10 MB wasm file is an assumption until the first deployment is measured. Brotli sizes are what a host that encoded with Brotli 11 would send; GitHub Pages does not.

Browser timings are desktop engines on a 20-CPU host, not phones. Chromium's CPU throttle does not reach a worker (the probe loop does not slow), so the slow-CPU configurations cap the whole container's CPU quota instead: an emulation that slows every browser thread together, pessimistic for a multi-core phone, calibrated by the probe loop. Neither is a phone measurement.

wasm_memory_bytes is the byte length of the instance's linear memory, read from the Emscripten module; resident memory is the sum of VmRSS of every process in the container except the driver, sampled every 100 ms.
The load average at the start and end is in the environment block; other work ran on the machine at the same time, so timings are indicative, not benchmark-grade.
